lessons.title: Advanced Swift: Generics, Protocols and Property Wrappers
lessons.description: Write reusable Swift with generics and constraints, protocols with associated types, protocol extensions, some and any, and your own property wrappers.

content.text: This course is for people who finished the beginner iOS course, or who already build small apps and want to work at the level a team expects. We start with the language, because most advanced iOS problems turn out to be language problems: how to write code once that works for many types, how to hide a repeated rule behind a clean name, and how to keep code safe when it grows. Lesson 1 covers the four tools that Apple's own frameworks use everywhere, and that interviewers ask about: generics, protocols with associated types, protocol extensions and property wrappers.
Generics: one function, many types

A **generic** function or type works with a placeholder type, written in angle brackets, instead of one fixed type. Swift fills in the real type at each use and checks it fully, so you get reuse without losing safety. You have already used generics without noticing: `[Expense]` is `Array<Expense>`, and `Optional<Int>` is `Int?`.

`T: Comparable` is a **constraint**: it says *T can be any type, as long as it can be compared*. Without it, the compiler would not let `max()` compile, because it cannot know that two Ts can be ordered. The `where Element: Equatable` extension adds `contains` only for stacks whose elements can be compared for equality, so a `Stack<Int>` gets it and a stack of non-equatable things does not.
Protocols with associated types

A plain protocol lists methods. A protocol can also name a placeholder type of its own, called an **associated type**. This is how you describe a *kind of thing that works with some type*, such as a repository that stores some kind of item.

The same protocol can be met by an in-memory version for tests, a SwiftData version for the app and a network version for a server, and `countItems` works with all of them. This is the heart of the *depend on protocols* idea from the first course, now with types that vary.
some and any

items: `some Repository` means *one specific type that I do not name, but the compiler knows*. SwiftUI's `some View` is the same idea. It is fast, because the real type is known at build time. A function that returns `some` must return one type from every path.

`any Repository` means *a box that can hold any type that meets the protocol*, and the real type is found at run time. It is more flexible, since you can put different types in one array, and a little slower. Swift 5.7 and later allow `any` with protocols that have associated types.
As a habit: use generics or `some` first, and use `any` when you really need to store different types together.

content.text: Protocol extensions: free behaviour

You can give every type that meets a protocol a ready-made method, by writing an extension on the protocol. Types may use it as it is, or write their own. Swift calls this style **protocol-oriented programming**. It is the reason that so much of the standard library comes with free helpers.

A subtle trap: if a method is only in the protocol *extension* and not in the protocol itself, Swift picks it by the *declared* type, and not by the real one. If a type is stored in a variable of the protocol type, the custom version is not called. List the method in the protocol itself when you want types to be able to replace it.
Property wrappers

A **property wrapper** moves the get and set rules of a property into a reusable type. You have used several: `@State`, `@Binding`, `@AppStorage`, `@Query`. Writing your own lets you hide a repeated rule, such as keeping a value in a range.

A wrapper may also offer a `projectedValue`, which you reach with a dollar sign. That is why `$title` gives a binding for `@State`: the `State` wrapper projects a `Binding`. Another feature you meet through SwiftUI is the **result builder**, written `@resultBuilder`. It lets many lines inside braces become one value, which is how a `VStack { ... }` collects its children. You rarely write one, and it helps to know where the magic comes from.
Key paths

A **key path** is a reference to a property, without reading it, written with a backslash: `\Expense.amount`. They are used by `@Query(sort:)` and by many APIs, and they can stand in for a closure, as in `expenses.map(\.amount)`.
Common mistakes

items: Over-generic code. If only one type will ever use a function, a generic only makes it harder to read. Reach for generics when you have a second real use.
Using `any` everywhere out of habit, and losing the speed and clarity of generics.
A property wrapper that hides work a reader would be surprised by. Keep wrappers small and obvious.

content.text: Your task

items: Write a generic `Stack<Element>` with `push`, `pop` and `top`, and test it with `Int` and `String`.
Add a `Repository` protocol and two types that meet it: an actor with an array, and one that stores to a dictionary by an `id`.
Write a `@Trimmed` property wrapper that removes spaces at both ends of a `String` every time it is set.
Use `map(\.amount)` and `sorted { $0.amount > $1.amount }` on an array of expenses, and write one sentence on what a key path is.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `largest(in:)` works for `Int` and `String` and returns `nil` for an empty array.
Setting `review.stars = 9` ends at 5, and your `@Trimmed` property removes spaces.
You can say, in your own words, the difference between `some` and `any`.

steps.say: A generic function is written once, with a placeholder type such as T.
A constraint says what T must be able to do, for example be compared.
Swift fills in Int where you call it with numbers, and checks every use.
The same code also works for String, with no copy and no loss of safety.

faqs.q: What is the difference between some and any in Swift?
faqs.a: some means one specific type that the compiler knows but you do not name. any means a box that can hold any type meeting the protocol, decided at run time. Prefer some or generics, and use any when you must mix types.

faqs.q: What is an associated type?
faqs.a: A placeholder type named inside a protocol, such as the Item a Repository stores. Each type that meets the protocol decides what the real type is.

faqs.q: What is a property wrapper?
faqs.a: A type that moves the get and set rules of a property into a reusable form. @State, @Binding and @AppStorage are property wrappers, and you can write your own.

quiz.q: What does the constraint in func largest<T: Comparable> do?
options: It says T can be any type that can be compared

quiz.q: What does some Repository mean?
options: One specific type the compiler knows but you do not name
A box that holds any type at run time
quiz.explain: any is the box that holds different types.

quiz.q: Which of these is a property wrapper?

notes: Generic = a placeholder type: `func largest<T: Comparable>(in: [T]) -> T?`. A constraint says what T can do.
`associatedtype` in a protocol = a placeholder the conforming type fills in (a Repository of some Item).
`some P` = one hidden type known at build time (fast). `any P` = a box for any type, decided at run time.
Protocol extension = free default behaviour. List a method in the protocol itself if types must be able to replace it.
Property wrapper = reusable get/set rules (@State, @Binding, own @Clamped). `$x` is the projected value.
Key path `\Expense.amount` refers to a property: `map(\.amount)`.

lessons.title: Advanced Swift Concurrency: TaskGroup, AsyncStream and Sendable
lessons.description: Run many tasks with TaskGroup, cancel work correctly, turn events into AsyncStream, and understand Sendable and strict concurrency in current Xcode versions.

content.text: The beginner course taught `async`, `await`, `Task` and actors. In real apps you also need to run a *variable* number of jobs at once, stop work that nobody wants any more, turn callbacks and events into a sequence you can loop over, and satisfy the compiler's checks for data races. These are the topics here, and they are all common in senior interviews.
TaskGroup: a variable number of tasks

`async let` is fine when you know how many calls there are. When you have a list, such as one request per account, use a **task group**. You add one child task per item. Child tasks run at the same time, and you collect results as they finish.

items: Results arrive in the order that tasks **finish**, and not the order you added them, so key them by an id, as above.
If one child throws, the group is cancelled and the error comes out of the `for try await` loop.
Do not start thousands of network calls at the same moment. Add a limit by starting a few tasks first and adding the next one each time one finishes.

content.text: Cancellation is cooperative

Cancelling a task does not stop it by force. It sets a flag, and the task must **look at the flag** and stop itself. Most Apple async APIs, such as `Task.sleep` and `URLSession`, check the flag for you and throw `CancellationError`. In your own long loops, check on purpose.
A very common real use is **search as you type**. Each key press cancels the previous search task and starts a new one after a short pause, so only the last word is searched.
AsyncStream: events as a sequence

An **AsyncSequence** is like an array whose items arrive over time. You loop over it with `for await`. `AsyncStream` lets you make one from your own source, such as a timer, a location update or an old delegate callback. You `yield` values into it, and `finish` when there are no more.

The `onTermination` closure cleans up when the reader stops, so the timer task does not run forever. The same idea turns a callback-based API, such as a location manager delegate, into a clean stream.
Sendable and strict concurrency

A type is **Sendable** when it is safe to pass between tasks, because nothing can be changed by two places at once. Value types made of Sendable parts, such as simple structs and enums, are Sendable. Actors are Sendable. A class is only Sendable if it is `final` and its stored properties are immutable (or protected). The compiler uses this to find data races *before* the app runs.

Swift 6 turned many of these checks from warnings into errors, if you choose the Swift 6 language mode, and recent Xcode versions add settings such as running code on the main actor by default in new projects. The details change between Xcode releases. A safe way to move an existing app: leave the language mode alone, turn on the extra checks one setting at a time in Build Settings, fix the warnings of one module at a time, and read Apple's migration guide for your Xcode version. Do not silence the checks with `@unchecked Sendable` unless you can explain why the type is really safe.
Actors: two more things to know

items: **Reentrancy:** when an actor method hits an `await`, other calls can run on the same actor before it continues. So state read before the `await` may have changed after it. Check again after the `await` when it matters.
**Global actors:** `@MainActor` is the one you know. You can make your own, but you rarely need to.
**`nonisolated`:** marks an actor member that does not touch the actor's data, so it can be called without `await`.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Starting a `Task` and forgetting to keep a reference, so it cannot be cancelled later.
Long loops that never check for cancellation.
Reading actor state before an `await` and trusting it after.
Using `@unchecked Sendable` to make a warning go away.

content.text: Your task

items: Write `totals(for:)` and call it with ten ids. Print the dictionary.
Make the search-as-you-type view, replace `search` with a function that waits for 200 ms, and watch earlier searches get cancelled.
Write `ticks(every:)` and read it with `for await`. Break after five ticks and confirm the timer task stops.
Make a struct and a final class that are `Sendable`, and write what would break if the class had a `var` property.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The group returns all ids even though tasks finish in a different order.
Typing quickly in the search box runs only the last search to the end.
You can explain what cooperative cancellation means and name one API that checks for it for you.

steps.say: The parent opens a task group and adds one child task for each item.
The child tasks run at the same time instead of one after another.
Results come back in the order the tasks finish, so key each one by an id.
If one child throws, the group is cancelled and the parent gets the error.

faqs.q: What is the difference between async let and a TaskGroup?
faqs.a: async let suits a fixed, small number of calls you can write out. A task group suits a list of any length, where you add one child task for each item and gather the results.

faqs.q: Does cancelling a Swift task stop it immediately?
faqs.a: No. Cancellation sets a flag and the task must check it. Many Apple APIs check for you and throw CancellationError. In your own loops, call Task.checkCancellation().

faqs.q: What does Sendable mean?
faqs.a: It marks a type that is safe to pass between tasks without data races. Simple value types and actors are Sendable, and classes must be final with immutable properties.

quiz.q: In what order do TaskGroup results arrive?
What does cancelling a task do?
options: Stops the task at once by force
Sets a flag the task must check

quiz.q: When is a class Sendable?
options: When it is final and its stored properties are immutable
When it has a var property

notes: `async let` = fixed number of calls. `withTaskGroup` = a list of any length. Results come in finish order, so key by id.
Cancellation is cooperative: `Task.checkCancellation()`, `Task.isCancelled`. Many Apple APIs check for you.
Search as you type: keep the Task, cancel it on each change, short sleep, check isCancelled.
`AsyncStream` makes events into a sequence for `for await`. Use `onTermination` to clean up.
Sendable = safe to pass between tasks. Structs of simple values, actors; classes must be final with immutable properties.
Actors are reentrant: state may change across an `await`. Avoid `@unchecked Sendable` as a quick fix.

lessons.title: Swift Memory Management: ARC, Retain Cycles and weak self
lessons.metaTitle: Swift ARC, Retain Cycles and weak self
lessons.description: Understand how ARC counts references to classes, spot and break retain cycles with weak and unowned, use capture lists, and find leaks with Instruments.

content.text: Swift manages memory for you, but not by magic. For **classes**, and for closures, it uses **Automatic Reference Counting**, or ARC. When your code does not follow its rules, the app **leaks** memory: objects that are never freed, so the app grows slowly until the system closes it. Memory questions are among the most common in iOS interviews, and leaks are among the most common real bugs, so the topic is worth an hour of care.
How ARC works

Each class instance has a counter of how many *strong* references point at it. When the counter reaches zero, Swift frees the object and calls its `deinit`. Structs and enums are values and are copied, so they do not have this problem. That is one more reason that SwiftUI uses structs for views.
Printing in `deinit` is the simplest leak detector you have. If a screen should be gone and you never see its message, something is still holding it.
The retain cycle
A **retain cycle** is two objects that hold strong references to each other, so neither count can reach zero. They keep each other alive for ever.

The fix is to make one side **weak**. A weak reference does not add to the count, and it becomes `nil` automatically when the object is freed, so it is always an optional `var`. Change the line to `weak var owner: Owner?`, and both messages print.

items: **`strong`** (the default) keeps the object alive.
**`weak`** does not keep it alive and becomes `nil` when the object goes. Use it when the other object can disappear first, such as a delegate or a parent.

**`unowned`** also does not keep it alive, but it is never `nil`. If the object is gone, using it crashes the app. Use it only when the two always live and die together, and when in doubt, use `weak`.

content.text: Closures and capture lists
A closure that uses `self` holds a strong reference to it. If `self` also holds the closure, you have a cycle. The cure is a **capture list**, written in square brackets before the closure's inputs.

`[weak self]` makes `self` optional inside the closure, and `guard let self else { return }` turns it back into a normal value for the rest of the closure. Not every closure needs this. A cycle exists only if the closure is stored somewhere that `self` owns. A closure passed to `map` or `sorted` is used once and thrown away, so it is safe.
Tasks and Combine

items: A `Task { ... }` that uses `self` keeps `self` alive until the task ends. If the task never ends, for example a loop over an `AsyncStream`, the object never goes. Use `[weak self]`, and make sure the task is cancelled when the object goes.
In Combine, a `sink` closure that uses `self` and is stored in `self`'s own set of cancellables is a classic cycle. Use `[weak self]` there too.
The SwiftUI `.task` modifier cancels itself when the view goes, which is another reason to prefer it.

content.text: Finding leaks

items: Add `deinit { print(...) }` to the classes you suspect, and navigate to the screen and back. No message means it did not free.
Run the app, open the screen several times, and use Xcode's **Debug Memory Graph** button in the debug bar. Leaked objects show a purple warning mark, and the graph shows what still points at them.

For a closer look, use **Instruments** (Product > Profile) with the **Leaks** and **Allocations** templates. Allocations shows how memory grows over time, and Leaks flags objects that cannot be reached.
Fix the cycle, then repeat the same steps and check that the message appears.

content.text: Some growth is not a leak. Caches, images and lists legitimately use memory. A leak is memory that grows each time you repeat the same action and never goes back down.
Common mistakes

items: Using `[weak self]` in every closure out of habit, which makes code noisy. Use it where a cycle can really form.
Using `unowned` to avoid writing the optional, and getting crashes later.
A delegate property declared without `weak`. Delegates should almost always be weak.
Believing that structs cannot leak. A struct that holds a reference to a class can still be part of a cycle.

content.text: Your task

items: Type the `Owner` and `Pet` classes, check that nothing is freed, then fix the cycle with `weak`.
Write the `Downloader` class both ways and see that only the weak version prints `Downloader freed`.
Open one of your own apps, add `deinit` prints to two view models, and check that they are freed when their screen closes.
Run the Debug Memory Graph on your app after opening the same screen five times.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Both `Owner freed` and `Pet freed` print after the fix.
You can explain in one sentence the difference between `weak` and `unowned`.
You can say when a closure needs a capture list and when it does not.

steps.say: Two objects each hold a strong reference to the other.
Their counts never reach zero, so neither is freed. The memory is leaked.
Marking one link weak means it no longer adds to the count.
When the last strong reference goes, both objects are freed and deinit runs.

faqs.q: What is a retain cycle in Swift?
faqs.a: Two class instances, or an object and a closure it stores, that hold strong references to each other. Their counts never reach zero, so they are never freed, and memory leaks.

faqs.q: What is the difference between weak and unowned?
faqs.a: Both avoid adding to the reference count. weak becomes nil when the object is freed, so it is an optional. unowned is never nil and crashes if the object is gone, so use it only when both live and die together.

faqs.q: Do I always need [weak self] in a closure?
faqs.a: No. You need it only when the closure is stored by something that self owns, so a cycle can form. A closure used once, such as in map, does not need it.

quiz.q: What is a retain cycle?
options: Objects holding strong references to each other so they are never freed

quiz.q: What happens if you use an unowned reference after its object is freed?
quiz.explain: weak becomes nil, unowned does not.

quiz.q: Which tool in Xcode helps find leaked objects?
options: Debug Memory Graph and Instruments Leaks

notes: ARC counts strong references to class instances. At zero the object is freed and `deinit` runs. Structs are copied.
Retain cycle = two objects (or an object and its closure) holding each other strongly. Never freed = leak.
`weak` = not counted, becomes nil, so an optional var. `unowned` = not counted, never nil, crashes if gone.
Closure stored by self: `[weak self] in guard let self else { return }`. A closure used once (map) is safe.
Delegates should be weak. Tasks and Combine sinks that use self can also cause cycles.
Find leaks: `deinit` prints, Debug Memory Graph (purple marks), Instruments Leaks and Allocations.

lessons.title: Combine in iOS: Publishers, sink, debounce and When to Use async
lessons.metaTitle: Combine in iOS: Publishers and sink
lessons.description: Learn the Combine basics you meet in real code: publishers, sink, operators, @Published, combineLatest and cancellables, and how it compares with async/await.

content.text: **Combine** is Apple's framework for handling values that change over time, such as text typed into a field, a stream of network results, or several inputs that must be checked together. It arrived in 2019, before async/await. Today, new code often uses async/await and `@Observable` instead, but Combine is still all over existing code bases, and the job posts that list *Combine* mean it. This lesson teaches you to read and write it, and to know when not to.
The three words: publisher, operator, subscriber

items: A **publisher** produces values over time, and may finish or fail.
An **operator** changes the values on their way: `map`, `filter`, `debounce`, `removeDuplicates`.
A **subscriber** receives the values. The simplest is `sink`, which runs a closure for each value.

content.text: Think of a pipe: a source, some filters in the middle, and a tap at the end. Nothing flows until a subscriber attaches.

import Combine

let subject = PassthroughSubject<String, Never>()
var cancellables = Set<AnyCancellable>()

subject
    .debounce(for: .milliseconds(300), scheduler: DispatchQueue.main)
    .removeDuplicates()
    .filter { $0.count >= 2 }
    .sink { text in
        print("search for", text)
    }
    .store(in: &cancellables)

subject.send("s")        // ignored: too short
subject.send("sw")
subject.send("swi")      // only the last value after 300 ms is delivered

`PassthroughSubject` is a publisher you can push values into by hand with `send`. The two type words say *the values are Strings* and *it never fails* (`Never`). `debounce` waits until values stop for a moment, which is the classic way to avoid a search call on every key press. `sink` returns an `AnyCancellable`. If you let it go, the subscription ends, so you keep it in a set with `store(in:)`.
@Published and ObservableObject

Before the `@Observable` macro, SwiftUI view models were classes that conformed to `ObservableObject`, with `@Published` properties. Every `@Published` property is a Combine publisher. You reach it with a dollar sign, and you can build pipes on top of it.

`CombineLatest` waits until each publisher has a value, then emits a new pair each time either one changes. The `map` turns each pair into one `Bool`, and `assign(to: &$isValid)` feeds it into the published property. The form is always up to date, with no manual code that runs on each change. In a view you use `@StateObject private var model = ExpenseFormModel()` to own such a class, where the newer `@Observable` classes use `@State`.
Networking with Combine

items: `receive(on:)` moves delivery to the main queue, which you need before touching the screen.
`eraseToAnyPublisher()` hides the long real type behind one simple name, so you can return it from a function.
A publisher can **fail**, and the failure arrives in `receiveCompletion`. After a failure the pipe is finished.

content.text: `someURL` and `Weather` are the URL and model from lesson 11 of the beginner course. Replace them with your own.
Combine or async/await?
Both can describe asynchronous work, and the choice is about the shape of the problem.

items: **One answer, later** (a network call, a database read): use `async/await`. It reads like normal code, and errors use `try` and `catch`.

**Many values over time, to be combined or timed** (typing with a pause, several inputs merged): Combine operators are strong here, and the same job in async code often needs more hand-written work. Swift also has `AsyncSequence` for streams, but fewer ready-made operators.
**Existing code:** if the project uses Combine, follow it. Rewriting working code for fashion is a risk with little gain.
You can move between them. A publisher has a `.values` property, so `for await value in subject.values { }` works, and `AsyncStream` can feed a publisher.

content.text: Apple's newer frameworks lean toward async/await and Observation. Learn Combine well enough to read and fix it, and use it for new work when its operators clearly make the code shorter.
Common mistakes

items: A `sink` that is not stored. The subscription ends at once, and nothing happens.
Updating the screen without `receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)`.
A `sink` that uses `self` and is stored in `self`'s cancellables, without `[weak self]`. This is a retain cycle from lesson 3.
Very long chains of operators that nobody can read. Split them and name the steps.

content.text: Your task

items: Type the debounce example in a Playground or a small app and check which values get through.
Build `ExpenseFormModel` and show a Save button that is disabled while `isValid` is false.
Write one `Publisher` for a URL as above, and also the same call with `async/await`. Compare the two in a few sentences.
Use `.values` to read a `PassthroughSubject` with `for await`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Only the last value after a pause reaches the `sink`.
The Save button turns on and off as you type.
You can say when you would pick async/await and when Combine.

steps.say: A publisher produces values over time, such as text typed in a field.
The debounce operator waits until the typing pauses.
The filter keeps only values that pass your test.
The sink subscriber receives what is left, and runs your closure. Keep its cancellable, or it stops.

faqs.q: What is Combine in iOS?
faqs.a: Apple's framework for handling values that change over time, built from publishers, operators and subscribers such as sink. It is common in existing code bases and has been joined by async/await and Observation.

faqs.q: Why must I store the result of sink?
faqs.a: sink returns an AnyCancellable. If it is released, the subscription ends. Storing it, usually in a Set<AnyCancellable> with store(in:), keeps the pipe alive.

faqs.q: Should I learn Combine in 2026 or only async/await?
faqs.a: Learn async/await first. Then learn enough Combine to read and maintain existing code, since many job posts and older projects still use it.

quiz.q: Why must you store the AnyCancellable from sink?
options: If it is released the subscription ends

quiz.q: What does debounce do?
options: Waits until values stop arriving for a moment

quiz.q: Which fits best for one answer later, such as a network call?

notes: Publisher makes values over time. Operator changes them (map, filter, debounce). Subscriber receives them (sink).
`sink` returns an AnyCancellable. Store it (`store(in: &cancellables)`) or the pipe stops.
`debounce` waits for a pause. `removeDuplicates`, `filter`, `CombineLatest` for forms.
`@Published` properties are publishers: use `$title`. `assign(to: &$isValid)` feeds a published property.
`receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)` before touching the UI. `eraseToAnyPublisher()` hides the long type.
One answer later: async/await. Many values over time: Combine. Follow the code base you work in.

lessons.title: Advanced SwiftUI: Modifiers, Custom Layout, Animation and Charts
lessons.description: Build reusable SwiftUI parts with ViewModifier and ViewBuilder, write a custom Layout, animate between states with matchedGeometryEffect, and draw charts.

content.text: Once you can build screens, the next skill is building **parts**: small, reusable pieces that give a whole app one consistent look and make each screen shorter. This lesson shows the SwiftUI tools for that, then two features that make apps feel polished: shared-element animation and charts. All of them need iOS 16 or newer, and most need nothing beyond what you already know.
ViewModifier: reuse a style
If you repeat the same chain of modifiers, such as padding, background, corners and shadow, wrap it in a `ViewModifier`. Add a small extension so the call reads like a built-in modifier.
ViewBuilder: containers that accept views
A view that takes other views as its content uses a **`@ViewBuilder`** property. This is how `VStack { ... }` works, and you can write your own.
A custom Layout

The `Layout` protocol (iOS 16 and up) lets you decide exactly how children are measured and placed, when stacks and grids are not enough. You write two methods: one that reports the total size, and one that places each child. This example makes every child as wide as the widest one.
Most layouts do not need a custom `Layout`. Try stacks, `Grid`, `LazyVGrid` and `ViewThatFits` first. Reach for `Layout` when you have a rule they cannot express, such as a wrapping row of tags.
matchedGeometryEffect: shared-element animation

`matchedGeometryEffect` tells SwiftUI that two views in different states are *the same thing*, so it moves and resizes one into the other. The classic use is a selection highlight that slides between tabs.

Only one capsule exists at a time, with the same `id` and `namespace`, so when `selected` changes SwiftUI animates it from the old place to the new one. The same idea can grow a thumbnail into a full-screen image.
Charts

Apple's **Charts** framework draws bar, line, area and other charts from your data in a few lines, with accessibility and Dark Mode built in. Each data point becomes a *mark*, and you say which values map to which axis.
Performance habits for SwiftUI

items: **Cheap bodies.** The `body` runs often. Do not sort big arrays, format many dates or decode JSON inside it. Compute once, and keep the result in state or the view model.
**Stable identity.** Give `ForEach` a stable `id`. An id that changes each time makes SwiftUI throw away and rebuild rows.
**Lazy containers.** Use `LazyVStack` or `List` for long content, and an ordinary `VStack` for a few views.
**Small views.** When one value changes, only the views that read it are redrawn. Splitting a big body into small views keeps redraws small.
**Measure, do not guess.** Xcode has a SwiftUI template in Instruments that shows how often views update.

content.text: Accessibility and Dark Mode in reusable parts

The great advantage of reusable parts is that you fix a problem once. Build accessibility into them from the start. In `CardStyle`, use semantic colours such as `.background` and `.primary`, so Dark Mode works without extra code. In a custom control, add `.accessibilityLabel("...")` and, where it makes sense, `.accessibilityAddTraits(.isButton)`. Text that uses `.font(.body)` or another text style grows when people choose larger text in Settings, so avoid fixed point sizes. Preview your parts in several settings at once, for example Dark Mode with the largest text size, using the Xcode preview variants. Ten minutes spent here saves many support emails later, and it is a point interviewers like to hear.
Common mistakes

items: Copying the same five modifiers on every screen instead of making a `ViewModifier`.
A `matchedGeometryEffect` where the same id appears twice at once, which confuses the animation.
Using `GeometryReader` for everything. It takes all the space it is given, and often a simpler tool is better.

content.text: Your task

items: Make `CardStyle` and `TitledCard` and use them on two screens of your app.
Write `EqualWidthHStack` and compare it with a normal `HStack` of two buttons with different text lengths.
Build the `PeriodPicker` and check that the highlight slides.
Draw the spending chart from your own expense data, grouped by category.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Changing `CardStyle` in one place changes every card.
The highlight moves smoothly between Day, Week and Month.
You can name three habits that keep a SwiftUI screen fast.

steps.say: You start with a plain view and a chain of modifiers you keep repeating.
You move the chain into a ViewModifier, written once.
A small extension gives it a short name such as card().
Every screen uses the same call, so one change updates the whole app.

faqs.q: When should I write a custom ViewModifier?
faqs.a: When you repeat the same chain of modifiers in several places. Put it in a ViewModifier and add a View extension so the call is short and the style lives in one place.

faqs.q: What is matchedGeometryEffect used for?
faqs.a: It tells SwiftUI that two views in different states are the same element, so it animates one into the other. A sliding tab highlight is a common example.

faqs.q: Which iOS version do the Charts framework and the Layout protocol need?
faqs.a: Both arrived in iOS 16, so they work if your minimum version is iOS 16 or newer.

quiz.q: When should you write a ViewModifier?
options: When you repeat the same chain of modifiers in several places

quiz.q: What does matchedGeometryEffect do?
options: Animates one view into another that is the same element in a new state

quiz.q: Which protocol lets you control exactly how children are measured and placed?

notes: `ViewModifier` + a `View` extension = one reusable style (`.card()`).
`@ViewBuilder var content: Content` lets your own container accept views in braces.
`Layout` protocol (iOS 16+): `sizeThatFits` and `placeSubviews`. Try stacks and Grid first.
`matchedGeometryEffect(id:in:)` with `@Namespace` animates one element between states.
Charts: `Chart(data) { BarMark(x: .value(...), y: .value(...)) }`.
Performance: cheap bodies, stable ids, lazy containers, small views, measure with Instruments.

lessons.title: SwiftUI Navigation at Scale: NavigationPath, Router, TabView and Deep Links
lessons.description: Control navigation from code with NavigationPath, build a small Router, organise an app with TabView, and open screens from deep links and Universal Links.

content.text: In the beginner course, a tap on a row pushed a screen. Real apps need more. A notification should open a particular expense. A button deep in a flow should jump back to the start. A link on a web page should open the app on the right screen. For all of these, navigation must be something your **code** can control, and not only the user's taps. This lesson shows how.
NavigationPath: the stack as data

`NavigationStack(path:)` takes a binding to the list of screens currently on the stack. If you change the list, the screens change. Push by appending, pop by removing, go back to the start by emptying it. `NavigationPath` holds values of mixed types, and an array works when all screens use one type.
Using one `Route` enum for the whole stack is a tidy habit. All the places you can go are listed in one type, and the `switch` makes sure every case has a screen.
A small Router
When many views need to navigate, hand them one shared object. With the `@Observable` macro from iOS 17, the object is a plain class, and any view that reads `path` redraws when it changes.

items: `.environment(router)` puts the router where every child can find it with `@Environment(Router.self)`.
`handle(_:)` reads a link such as `expensetracker://expense/<id>`, empties the stack, then pushes the target. Starting from a clean stack avoids odd back buttons.
This is the idea behind the **Coordinator** pattern from UIKit, in a smaller form. One object decides where the app goes, and screens only ask.

content.text: `ExpenseScreen`, `SettingsScreen`, `CategoryScreen` and `HomeView` in this example are small views you write yourself. Any placeholder `Text` view will do while you test.
TabView
A `TabView` gives an app its tab bar. Each tab usually has its own `NavigationStack` with its own history, so switching tabs does not lose your place.

Because the selection is a value, a deep link can also switch tabs by setting `selection`. Newer iOS versions add a new `Tab` type for building tab bars. The `tabItem` form above works on all the versions this course targets.
Deep links

items: **Custom URL scheme** such as `expensetracker://expense/123`. In Xcode, open your target, then **Info > URL Types**, and add the scheme. Easy to set up, but any app can claim the same scheme.

**Universal Links** such as `https://example.com/expense/123`. The web address opens your app if it is installed, and the website if not. You add the **Associated Domains** capability with `applinks:example.com`, and host an `apple-app-site-association` file on your website, over HTTPS, listing the paths your app handles. The details of the file are in Apple's documentation and change with iOS versions, so read the current page before you set it up.
Both arrive in SwiftUI through `.onOpenURL`, as above. Notification taps usually carry a URL or an id in their payload, which you hand to the same `handle` function.

content.text: Treat every incoming link as **untrusted input**. A link can be made by anyone. Check the scheme, the host and the format of each part, and never run actions such as deleting or paying straight from a link without asking the user.
Keeping place: state restoration

People expect to come back to where they were. `@SceneStorage` keeps small values, such as the selected tab, across launches of a scene, and `NavigationPath` has a `codable` form you can save and restore when all your route types are `Codable`. Use it for the main flows, and do not worry about restoring every sheet.
Common mistakes

items: A route enum that holds big objects. Put an id in the route and load the object in the destination.
Two `NavigationStack`s nested by accident, which gives two title bars.
Opening a link without checking that the data still exists. Show a clear *not found* message.

content.text: Your task

items: Add a `Route` enum and a `Router` to your Expense Tracker.
Register the URL scheme and test it in the Simulator with `xcrun simctl openurl booted "expensetracker://expense/<an id from your data>"`.
Put the app in a `TabView` with a separate stack in each tab.
Add a *popToRoot* button on a detail screen and check that it works from three levels deep.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Opening the link in the Simulator shows the right expense, even from another tab or screen.
Each tab keeps its own history.
You can say why an incoming link must be treated as untrusted input.

animation.title: Open a screen from a link

steps.say: A link arrives from a notification, a web page or another app.
SwiftUI passes it to onOpenURL.
The router checks the scheme, host and id, then clears the stack and appends a route.
The navigation stack shows the screen for that route.

faqs.q: What is NavigationPath in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: A list of the screens currently on a NavigationStack. Changing it from code pushes or pops screens, which lets you navigate from notifications, links and buttons deep in a flow.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a URL scheme and a Universal Link?
faqs.a: A URL scheme is a custom prefix such as myapp:// that any app may claim. A Universal Link is a normal https address that opens your app if installed and the website if not, and it needs a file on your domain and the Associated Domains capability.

faqs.q: Do I need the Coordinator pattern in SwiftUI?
faqs.a: Usually not in its UIKit form. A small Router with a NavigationPath gives the same benefit, one place that decides where the app goes.

quiz.q: What does changing a NavigationPath from code do?
options: Pushes or pops screens on the stack

quiz.q: How should an app treat an incoming deep link?
options: As a command to run at once

quiz.q: Which SwiftUI modifier receives a URL that opened the app?

notes: `NavigationStack(path: $path)` makes the stack data. Append to push, remove to pop, empty it to go home.
One `Route: Hashable` enum lists every destination. `navigationDestination(for:)` switches on it.
A small `@Observable` Router shared with `.environment(router)` is the SwiftUI version of Coordinator.
`TabView` with a NavigationStack in each tab. Selection is a value, so a link can switch tabs.
Deep links: URL scheme (any app can claim it) or Universal Links (https, Associated Domains, a file on your site). Arrive in `.onOpenURL`.
Treat every link as untrusted input. Check scheme, host and id. Put ids, not big objects, in routes.

lessons.title: UIKit for SwiftUI Developers: Interop, Auto Layout and Table Views
lessons.description: Learn the UIKit you will meet at work: view controller life cycle, Auto Layout in code, diffable table views, and mixing UIKit with SwiftUI in both directions.

content.text: Many companies started their apps before SwiftUI existed, and a rewrite is rarely worth the risk. If you join such a team, most of your day is in **UIKit**. Even a brand new SwiftUI app will use UIKit through the camera, the map or a text view that SwiftUI does not cover well. This lesson gives you enough UIKit to read a code base, fix a bug and add a screen. It does not try to teach all of it.
The mental model

items: A screen is a **view controller** (`UIViewController`). It owns a **view**, which owns smaller views.
UIKit is **imperative**: you create views, set properties, and change them yourself when data changes. SwiftUI describes the result, and UIKit gives the steps.
UIKit is built on classes, so the memory rules of lesson 3 apply. Delegates must be `weak`, and closures stored on the controller need `[weak self]`.

content.text: The view controller life cycle

The order matters in interviews and in bugs. Set things up once in `viewDidLoad`. Refresh in `viewWillAppear`, which runs again when the user comes back with the back button. Do not measure sizes in `viewDidLoad`, because the layout is not final there.
Auto Layout in code

**Auto Layout** places views with *constraints*, rules such as *this label's top is 16 points below the safe area* and *this button is centred*. You can set them in Interface Builder (a storyboard or a `.xib` file), or in code. Code is easier to review in Git and to merge between people, and many teams prefer it.

items: Always set `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false` on views you constrain yourself. Forgetting it is the most common Auto Layout bug.
Give every view enough constraints to know its **position and size**. If the console prints *Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints*, two rules disagree, and the message names them.
Use `UIStackView` for rows and columns, as you would `HStack` and `VStack`.
Use `.preferredFont(forTextStyle:)` so text follows the user's size setting.

content.text: A table view with a diffable data source

`UITableView` is the ancestor of `List`. The modern way to feed it is a **diffable data source**. You give it a *snapshot*, a description of what should be shown, and it works out what to insert, delete and move, with animation. This replaces the old index-path bookkeeping that caused many crashes.

`dequeueReusableCell` is the key idea of table views. The table does not create a cell for every row. It reuses the few cells that are on screen, which keeps long lists fast. This is also why a cell must be fully set up each time it is configured. A leftover value from the previous row is a classic bug.
SwiftUI inside UIKit, and UIKit inside SwiftUI
Both directions are supported, so you can move an app screen by screen.

items: `UIViewRepresentable` has `makeUIView` (create once) and `updateUIView` (called when SwiftUI state changes). The **Coordinator** is a helper class that receives UIKit's delegate and target-action calls and passes them back through the binding.
`UIViewControllerRepresentable` is the same idea for a whole view controller, such as a camera picker.
`UIHostingController` is a view controller that shows a SwiftUI view.

content.text: Core Animation and UIView animation

UIKit views are backed by **layers** from Core Animation. For simple changes, you rarely need to touch them. `UIView.animate` animates changes to properties such as `alpha`, `frame` and `transform`. When you need more, such as a pulsing effect, use a `CABasicAnimation` on the layer.

UIView.animate(withDuration: 0.3) {
    badgeView.alpha = 1
    badgeView.transform = CGAffineTransform(scaleX: 1.2, y: 1.2)
}

let pulse = CABasicAnimation(keyPath: "transform.scale")
pulse.fromValue = 1.0
pulse.toValue = 1.15
pulse.duration = 0.6
pulse.autoreverses = true
pulse.repeatCount = .infinity
badgeView.layer.add(pulse, forKey: "pulse")
Common mistakes

items: A delegate property that is not `weak`, which leaks the controller.
Changing the screen from a background thread. UIKit must be used on the main thread.
Heavy work in `cellForRowAt` or in the diffable data source closure, which makes scrolling jerky.
Mixing manual `frame` values with Auto Layout on the same view.

content.text: Your task

items: Make a view controller with a label and a button laid out with constraints, and check it in a small and a large iPhone.
Build the diffable table view and add a button that appends a new item with animation.
Wrap `UITextField` in `UIViewRepresentable` and use it in a SwiftUI form.
Show a SwiftUI view inside a `UIHostingController` pushed from a UIKit screen.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The constraints give no warnings in the console on any iPhone size.
A new item appears in the table with an animation, and no manual index paths are used.
You can list the life cycle methods in the order they run, and say what belongs in each.

steps.say: An older UIKit app is made of view controllers.
A UIHostingController lets a UIKit screen show a SwiftUI view, so new screens can use SwiftUI.
The SwiftUI view runs inside it as normal.
The other way round, UIViewRepresentable wraps a UIKit view for use in SwiftUI.

faqs.q: Do I still need to learn UIKit in 2026?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to work on existing apps. Many companies still have large UIKit code bases, and even SwiftUI apps use UIKit for features SwiftUI does not cover well.

faqs.q: What is a diffable data source?
faqs.a: A modern way to feed a table or collection view with a snapshot of what should be shown. It works out the inserts, deletes and moves for you, with animation, and avoids index-path bugs.

faqs.q: What is the Coordinator in UIViewRepresentable?
faqs.a: A helper class that receives UIKit delegate and target-action calls and passes the results back to SwiftUI, for example by updating a binding.

quiz.q: Where should you set up subviews once in a view controller?
What does UIHostingController do?
options: Shows a SwiftUI view inside UIKit

quiz.q: What must you set to false on a view you constrain in code?

notes: Life cycle: viewDidLoad (once), viewWillAppear (every time), viewDidAppear, viewWillDisappear.
Auto Layout = constraints. In code set `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false`, then `NSLayoutConstraint.activate`.
Table view: `dequeueReusableCell` reuses cells. Configure the whole cell each time.
Diffable data source: apply a snapshot, UIKit works out inserts, deletes and moves.
SwiftUI in UIKit: `UIHostingController`. UIKit in SwiftUI: `UIViewRepresentable` with a Coordinator.
Delegates weak, UI on the main thread. `UIView.animate` for simple changes, `CABasicAnimation` for layers.

lessons.title: A Production Networking Layer: Auth Tokens, Retry, Keychain and Face ID
lessons.metaTitle: iOS Networking Layer, Keychain and Auth
lessons.description: Build a clean API client with endpoints, token refresh and retry, store secrets in the Keychain, add Face ID, and know the rules for Sign in with Apple.

content.text: The weather call in the beginner course was fine for a demo. A real app calls dozens of endpoints, signs requests with a token that expires, survives bad connections, and must keep that token somewhere safe. If each screen builds its own request, the code becomes copy and paste, and bugs multiply. This lesson builds the layer that sits between screens and the network, and then the safe storage and sign-in pieces around it.
Describe endpoints as values
Instead of building URLs inside each view model, describe each call in one place, as a small type. Then one client sends them all.
The protocol extension from lesson 1 supplies defaults, so a simple endpoint needs only a path. Adding an endpoint is now a few lines in one file, and a view model never sees a URL.
One client for all calls

items: **Retry only what can succeed on a second try.** Server errors (5xx) and timeouts may. A 400 or 404 will fail again, so do not retry them.
**Back off.** Wait longer after each failure, here 2 s and then 4 s. Hammering a struggling server makes it worse.
**Never retry a request that changes data** (a payment, a purchase) unless the server supports an *idempotency key*, so a repeat cannot charge twice.
**Set a timeout** so a slow connection ends in an error and not an endless spinner.

content.text: Refreshing the token once, not ten times

An access token expires, and a refresh token gets a new one. If ten requests start at once with an expired token, you do not want ten refresh calls. An **actor** is the right tool: it holds one shared refresh task, and every caller waits for the same one.

The `refresh()` body above is a placeholder, because every server has its own refresh call. Notice the check after the `await`: the actor is *reentrant*, as lesson 2 explained, so the shared `refreshTask` is what stops two refreshes from running at once.
The Keychain: where secrets live

Never keep tokens, passwords or keys in `UserDefaults`, in a plain file or in the code. Those are easy to read from a backup or a device that has been opened. The **Keychain** is the system's encrypted store for small secrets, and it is the correct place. Its API is old and written in C, so most teams wrap it in a small type, as below.

Replace the service name with your own bundle identifier. The setting `WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` means that the item is readable only while the phone is unlocked and is not copied to other devices through a backup. Log out by deleting the item.
Face ID and Touch ID

The `LocalAuthentication` framework asks the system to check the person's face or fingerprint. You never see the biometric data. You only learn whether it worked. You must add a short **Face ID usage description** to your app's Info settings, or the app will be stopped when it asks.
`.deviceOwnerAuthentication` lets the person fall back to the device passcode if the face or finger does not work. That is kinder and safer than blocking them.
Sign in with Apple, and other rules

items: **Sign in with Apple** lets people create an account without sharing their email address. SwiftUI has a ready-made `SignInWithAppleButton`, and it needs the *Sign in with Apple* capability in your target. Apple's App Review Guidelines may require you to offer it if your app offers other third-party sign-in options. Read the current guideline before you submit.
**Account deletion:** Apple requires apps that let people create an account to also let them delete it from inside the app. Check the current rules and plan this early.
**HTTPS only.** App Transport Security blocks plain `http`. Avoid turning it off.
**Certificate pinning** (only trusting your own server's certificate) can add safety for banking-like apps, but it also breaks when you change certificates. Use it only if you can manage that.
**Do not log secrets.** Never print tokens or passwords, even in debug builds.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Tokens in `UserDefaults`.
Retrying a payment request automatically.
Ten parallel refresh calls, because the refresh is not shared.
Showing the user a raw error such as `badStatus(500)`. Map errors to messages a person can act on.

content.text: Your task

items: Make `Endpoint`, three endpoints of your own and the `APIClient`. Point it at any test server you have or at a local mock.
Write the `TokenStore` actor and test it by starting five requests at once. Print how many times `refresh()` ran. It should be once.
Store a fake token in the Keychain, read it back, then delete it.
Add a biometric unlock before a *settings* screen, and add the Face ID usage description.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A 503 response is retried twice with a delay, and a 404 is not retried.
Five simultaneous calls cause one refresh.
The token survives an app restart and is gone after logout.

steps.say: A view model asks the client for an endpoint. It never builds a URL.
The client builds the request and asks the token store for a valid token.
The token comes from the Keychain, the encrypted store for small secrets.
The client sends the request. A temporary server error is retried with a delay, a client error is not.

faqs.q: Where should an iOS app store an access token?
faqs.a: In the Keychain, the system's encrypted store for small secrets. Do not use UserDefaults or plain files, which are easy to read from a backup.

faqs.q: Which failed requests should be retried automatically?
faqs.a: Ones that can succeed on a second try, such as server errors (5xx) and timeouts, with a growing delay. Do not retry client errors such as 400 or 404, and do not retry requests that change money or data without an idempotency key.

faqs.q: Is Sign in with Apple required?
faqs.a: Apple's App Review Guidelines may require it if your app offers other third-party sign-in options, and they also require account deletion inside apps that create accounts. Rules change, so read the current guidelines before you submit.

quiz.q: Where should an access token be stored?
Which failed request is worth retrying automatically?
quiz.explain: Use a growing delay, and never auto-retry a payment without an idempotency key.

quiz.q: Why use an actor to refresh a token?
options: So many callers share one refresh instead of making ten

notes: Describe each call as an `Endpoint` value. One `APIClient` sends them all, so view models never build URLs.
Retry only what can succeed (5xx, timeouts), with backoff (2 s, 4 s). Never auto-retry payments without an idempotency key.
A `TokenStore` actor shares one refresh task, so ten calls cause one refresh.
Secrets belong in the Keychain (`SecItemAdd`, `SecItemCopyMatching`), never in UserDefaults or code.
Face ID: `LAContext.evaluatePolicy`, plus the Face ID usage description. Allow passcode fallback.
Sign in with Apple and in-app account deletion may be required by App Review. Read the current rules. Never log tokens.

lessons.title: SwiftData in Depth: Relationships, Migrations, Background Work and iCloud
lessons.description: Model related data with SwiftData relationships, fetch with FetchDescriptor, plan schema migrations, import on a background actor, and learn iCloud sync rules.

content.text: In the beginner course SwiftData saved one kind of object. A real app has related data: an account has many entries, a category has many expenses, a recipe has ingredients. And real apps live for years, so the shape of the data changes after people already have data on their phones. This lesson covers the three problems that come with that: **relationships**, **migrations** and **work off the main thread**, plus the rules for syncing with iCloud. Because Apple changes these APIs between releases, read the current documentation for your Xcode version, and treat the code here as the shape of the solution.
Relationships

A relationship is a property that points to another model, or to a list of them. Mark the owning side with `@Relationship`, say what happens to the children when the parent is deleted, and name the property on the other side with `inverse`, so both sides stay in step.

items: `deleteRule: .cascade` deletes the entries when the account is deleted. `.nullify` (the default) keeps the entries and clears their link. `.deny` refuses to delete an account that still has entries. Pick the one that matches what the user expects.
Set the link on **one** side and SwiftData updates the other: `entry.account = cash` makes `cash.entries` include the entry.
The `Account?` is optional because an entry may exist before it has an account, and because iCloud sync needs optional relationships.
`@Attribute(.unique)` makes a property unique across the store, such as an email address. Note that unique constraints cannot be used with iCloud sync.

content.text: Fetching with FetchDescriptor
`@Query` is for views. In other code, such as a view model, an import job or a test, you fetch with a `FetchDescriptor` and the model context. It lets you set the filter, the order and a limit.
A `fetchLimit` matters for large tables. Loading ten thousand rows to show twenty wastes time and memory. Add an index or a limit before you reach for caching.
Migrations: changing the model after release

When you add a property with a default value, SwiftData can usually migrate the store by itself. Bigger changes, such as renaming a property, splitting one model into two or changing a type, need a **versioned schema** and a **migration plan**. You freeze each shipped version of the model in its own type, and describe how to move from one to the next.

items: A **lightweight** stage handles simple changes, such as adding a property with a default. A **custom** stage lets you run your own code before and after, for harder changes.

**Test migrations with real data.** Install the old version of your app, add data, then install the new version over it. A migration that fails can stop the app from opening, which is among the worst bugs a release can have.
**Never edit a shipped schema version.** Add a new one.

content.text: Work off the main thread: ModelActor

A big import, such as ten thousand rows from a server, must not freeze the screen. SwiftData provides `@ModelActor`, a macro that makes an actor with its own model context. Work done inside it stays off the main actor.

Objects belong to the context that made them. Do not pass a model object between actors. Pass its `persistentModelID` or the plain values, and fetch it again where you need it. SwiftUI's `@Query` will pick up the saved changes by itself.
Syncing with iCloud

SwiftData can sync a private database through **CloudKit**, Apple's iCloud service, and the people using the app pay nothing for the storage. You add the **iCloud** capability with CloudKit and the **Background Modes** capability with *Remote notifications*, and create the container with a CloudKit configuration. Apple's documentation lists the rules your models must follow. The main ones are that every property needs a default value or must be optional, relationships must be optional, and unique constraints are not allowed. It is easier to design for these from the start than to change a shipped model later.

Sync brings new problems: two devices editing the same item, a user who is signed out of iCloud, and a first launch with no network. Test with two devices or two simulators signed in to the same account, and show the user honest messages when sync is off.
Where Core Data and other options fit

items: **Core Data** is the older framework under SwiftData. Apps that started before iOS 17 use it, and it supports iOS versions that SwiftData does not. Its ideas are the same: a container, contexts, fetch requests, migrations.
**SQLite** libraries such as GRDB suit teams that want full control of SQL. They are a good choice when you need very complex queries.

**A backend** such as Firebase or your own server holds data that must be shared between *people*, not only between one person's devices. The app often keeps a local copy as well, so it works offline.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Loading all rows when the screen shows twenty.
Changing a shipped model with no migration.
Passing model objects between actors.
Forgetting what the delete rule does, and removing more data than the user expected.

content.text: Your task

items: Add `Account` and `Entry` with a relationship. Delete an account and check what happens to its entries with `.cascade` and then `.nullify`.
Write a `fetchLimit` query for the 20 newest entries over a given amount.
Create `SchemaV1` and `SchemaV2` as above and write down the exact steps you would use to test the migration with real data.
Write the `@ModelActor` importer and import 5,000 rows while a list is on screen. The screen should stay responsive.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The delete rule behaves as you expect in both modes.
The list stays responsive during the import.
You can say three rules a model must follow to sync with iCloud.

steps.say: Real users already have data stored in version 1 of your model.
A migration plan says how to move from one version to the next.
Version 2 is a new, separate schema. You never edit a shipped version.
The updated app opens with the old data intact. Always test this with real data first.

faqs.q: When do I need a SwiftData migration plan?
faqs.a: When you change a shipped model in a way SwiftData cannot handle automatically, such as renaming a property or splitting a model. Adding a property with a default value is often handled for you. Test with real data before every release.

faqs.q: What does a relationship delete rule do?
faqs.a: It says what happens to related objects when the parent is deleted. Cascade deletes them, nullify keeps them and clears the link, and deny refuses to delete the parent while children exist.

faqs.q: How do I import a lot of data without freezing the app?
faqs.a: Use a ModelActor, which has its own model context and runs off the main actor. Pass plain values in and do not move model objects between actors.

quiz.q: What does deleteRule .cascade do?
options: Keeps the related objects and clears the link
Deletes the related objects when the parent is deleted

quiz.q: How do you import thousands of rows without freezing the screen?
options: Use a ModelActor with its own context
Use the main context in a loop

quiz.q: Which is a rule for syncing a model with iCloud?
options: No property may have a default

notes: `@Relationship(deleteRule:inverse:)`: cascade deletes children, nullify clears the link, deny blocks the delete.
`FetchDescriptor` with predicate, sort and `fetchLimit` for fetching outside views.
Migration: freeze each shipped model in a `VersionedSchema`, plan the steps in a `SchemaMigrationPlan`. Never edit a shipped version.
Test migrations with real data from the old app version.
`@ModelActor` gives an actor with its own context for big imports. Do not pass model objects between actors.
iCloud sync: properties need defaults or optional, relationships optional, no unique constraints. Check Apple docs.

lessons.title: Core Location, MapKit and Push Notifications in iOS
lessons.description: Ask for location permission properly, show places on a SwiftUI map, search nearby, schedule local notifications and learn how push and background tasks work.

content.text: Apps feel native when they use the phone: where you are, what is nearby, and a reminder at the right moment. These features share two things. They touch **private data or attention**, so Apple requires a permission and an honest reason. And they depend on the system, which decides when your code runs. This lesson covers location, maps and notifications, with the permission rules first.
Permissions: the rules for all private features

items: Every private feature needs a **usage description** in the app's Info settings, a short sentence that says *why*, such as *Used to show expenses near you*. Without it, the app is stopped at the moment you ask. Reviewers also read these sentences.
Ask **at the moment the feature is needed**, not at launch. A person who sees *Allow location?* right after opening the app, with no context, often says no.
Always handle **no**. A good app still works, with a clear way to change the setting later.
Ask for the **least** you need. *While Using the App* is enough for most apps.

content.text: Core Location

Add the key `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` to your target's Info settings. The delegate methods tell you when the person answers and when a position arrives. Choose the lowest accuracy that does the job, and ask for **one** position with `requestLocation()` when you only need one, because GPS drains the battery. Newer iOS versions also offer an async way to read location updates (`CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates()`), which is worth learning once you know this delegate version.

Delegate callbacks and Swift's strict concurrency checks can disagree in newer language modes. If Xcode reports main-actor warnings on this class, mark the class `@MainActor` and the delegate methods `nonisolated`, and hop back to the main actor to set properties. Follow the message the compiler gives for your Xcode version.
MapKit in SwiftUI
From iOS 17, SwiftUI has a `Map` view you fill with *markers* and *annotations*, written like any other SwiftUI content.
`UserAnnotation` shows the blue dot once you have permission. To find places, use `MKLocalSearch`, which searches Apple's map data.
Local notifications

A **local notification** is scheduled by your app on the device, with no server. It suits reminders, such as *log today's expenses at 8 pm*. First ask for permission, then schedule a request with a trigger.

items: Using the same `identifier` again replaces the old request, so a person does not get two reminders.
By default, a notification does **not** show while your app is open. If you want it to, set a `UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate` and return the options you want from `willPresent`.
Give people a way to turn reminders off inside the app, in addition to the system settings.

content.text: Push notifications

A **push notification** is sent from your server, through Apple's service, **APNs**. The path is: your app asks the system to register, the system gives the app a **device token**, the app sends that token to your server, and the server asks APNs to deliver a message to that token. For the server to talk to APNs you create an **authentication key** (a `.p8` file) in your Apple developer account. You add the **Push Notifications** capability to the app.

Device tokens can change, so send the token to your server each time the app launches and the person is signed in. Never put the APNs key in the app. It belongs only on your server. Push does not work in some Simulator set-ups and is best tested on a real device. Check Apple's current notes.
Background work

iOS stops an app soon after the person leaves it, to save battery. For work that must happen anyway, such as refreshing data, you do not run code yourself. You **ask the system**, and it decides when. `BGTaskScheduler` lets you register a refresh task, and the system runs it at a time it picks, which may be late, or not at all if the battery is low. A push with `content-available` can also wake the app briefly. Always design the app so that it **works correctly when no background work ran**, and treat background work as a bonus.
Common mistakes

items: Asking for permission on first launch with no context.
No handling for *denied*. The feature silently does nothing.
Keeping GPS on all the time.
Putting server secrets in the app, or expecting background tasks to run at an exact time.

content.text: Your task

items: Add the location usage description, ask for permission from a button, and show the coordinates.
Show a `Map` with one marker and the user's location, and search for *coffee* nearby.
Schedule the daily reminder from a toggle in a settings screen, and cancel it when the toggle is off.
Write down the steps of a push notification from your app to a phone, in order, in your own words.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Denying permission shows a helpful message and the app keeps working.
The reminder arrives at the chosen time, and only one is scheduled.
You can explain why the APNs key must stay on the server.

steps.say: After the person allows notifications, the app registers and the system gives it a device token.
The app sends the token to your server, which stores it with the user.
When something happens, your server asks APNs to deliver a message to that token. The key stays on the server.
APNs delivers it, and the phone shows the notification.

faqs.q: When should an app ask for location permission?
faqs.a: At the moment the feature is needed, with a clear reason in the usage description, and for the least access you need. Always handle the case where the person says no.

faqs.q: What is the difference between local and push notifications?
faqs.a: A local notification is scheduled by the app on the device with no server. A push notification is sent by your server through Apple's APNs service to the device token.

faqs.q: Can I rely on background tasks running at a set time?
faqs.a: No. You ask the system, and it decides when, or whether, to run them. Design the app to work correctly even if no background work happened.

quiz.q: When should you ask for location permission?
options: When the feature is first needed, with a clear reason

quiz.q: Where does the APNs key belong?
Can you rely on a background task running at an exact time?
options: No, the system decides when or whether it runs

notes: Every private feature needs a usage description. Ask when needed, handle "no", ask for the least access.
Core Location: `CLLocationManager`, `requestWhenInUseAuthorization()`, `requestLocation()` for one fix.
SwiftUI `Map` with `Marker` and `UserAnnotation` (iOS 17). `MKLocalSearch` finds places.
Local notification: `UNUserNotificationCenter`, content plus trigger plus request. Same identifier replaces the old one.
Push: app registers, gets a device token, sends it to your server, server asks APNs. The APNs key stays on the server.
Background tasks: you ask the system, it decides when. The app must work if none ran.

lessons.title: Apple Frameworks Tour: StoreKit 2, Vision, AVFoundation and HealthKit
lessons.description: Sell in-app purchases with StoreKit 2, read text from images with Vision, play media with AVFoundation, and learn the permission rules of HealthKit.

content.text: Apple provides a framework for nearly every device feature, and job posts list the names: StoreKit, Vision, AVFoundation, HealthKit. You will not master them all, and you do not need to. What you need is to know **what each one is for**, to be able to start one using the documentation, and to know the rules that come with it. This lesson gives a working first step in each of four of the most requested ones.
StoreKit 2: in-app purchases

**StoreKit** lets you sell things inside your app: a one-time unlock, a consumable such as credits, or an auto-renewing subscription. You create the products in App Store Connect with a product id, a price tier and a description. In the app, you fetch them, show them and start the purchase. StoreKit 2 is the Swift-first version that uses async/await.

items: `purchase()` returns a result. Only treat a purchase as real when its `verification` is `.verified`. StoreKit 2 checks Apple's signature for you.
Call `transaction.finish()` after you have given the person what they bought.
`Transaction.currentEntitlements` lists what the person owns now. Check it at launch, so a purchase made on another device, or a refund, is reflected.
Also listen to `Transaction.updates` in a long-running task, to catch purchases that finish later, for example after a *Ask to Buy* approval.

Test with a **StoreKit configuration file** in Xcode, which pretends to be the store, so you can test purchases, refunds and renewals with no real money. Then test with a Sandbox account before release.

content.text: Apple's guidelines say what you must offer and show for purchases and subscriptions. Examples are a *Restore Purchases* path, clear price and renewal text, and rules about which things must use in-app purchase. Read the current guideline on in-app purchase before you design the screen, because rules and fees change.
Vision: reading what is in an image

**Vision** analyses images on the device: text, faces, barcodes, body poses and more. Nothing needs to be sent to a server, which is good for privacy and works offline. Here is text recognition, the *scan a receipt* feature that fits our Expense Tracker.

This also shows a useful pattern. Vision uses a completion handler, an older style, so we wrap it in `withCheckedThrowingContinuation` to make it `async`. You will do the same with many older Apple APIs. The continuation must be resumed **exactly once**. The result is a list of text lines. Finding the *total* in a receipt from those lines is your own logic, and you should always let the user check and correct what was read.
AVFoundation: audio, video and the camera
**AVFoundation** is the large framework for media. At the simplest level, playing a video in SwiftUI takes a few lines with `AVKit`.

items: **Playing sound:** `AVAudioPlayer` for short files, `AVPlayer` for streams and video.
**Audio sessions:** `AVAudioSession` tells the system whether your app should play over other music, mute with the silent switch, or record.

**The camera:** `AVCaptureSession` with an input and an output gives full control, and needs `NSCameraUsageDescription`. If you only need a photo, the system's `PhotosPicker` and camera picker are much simpler, and need less permission.

content.text: HealthKit

**HealthKit** reads and writes health data that the person keeps on the device, such as steps, sleep and workouts. The rules are the strictest of the frameworks here. You add the HealthKit capability, write a usage description that says exactly why you read each type, and ask for each kind of data separately. The person may allow some and not others, and your app cannot even tell whether *reading* was denied. Apple's guidelines restrict how health data may be used, for example it must not be used for advertising, so read them before you design a feature.
How to learn a new framework

items: Read the framework's overview page and look for a sample app from Apple.
Add the capability and usage description first. Many first-run crashes are a missing description.
Get the smallest result working, like one marker or one text line, before you design the screen.
Wrap the framework in your own small type, as with `Store` above, so the rest of the app does not depend on its details and you can fake it in tests.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Granting a purchase without checking `.verified`.
A purchase flow with no *Restore Purchases* option.
Resuming a continuation twice, or never. Both are bugs.
Collecting health or location data you do not need.

content.text: Your task

items: Create a StoreKit configuration file with one non-consumable product, run the `Store` class and buy it in the Simulator.
Add a *Restore Purchases* button that calls `AppStore.sync()` and then refreshes the entitlements.
Use `recognizeText(in:)` on a photo of a printed receipt and list the lines in a `List`.
Write one sentence for each framework in this lesson: what it is for, and one rule that comes with it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The purchase works in the configuration file and `isPro` stays on after relaunch.
The recognised lines appear, and you can correct them by hand.
You can explain why a continuation must be resumed exactly once.

steps.say: Your screen shows the product fetched from the App Store.
The person taps Buy, and StoreKit starts the purchase.
The result carries a verification. Only a verified transaction counts.
You unlock the feature and call finish(). At each launch, currentEntitlements keeps it right.

faqs.q: What is StoreKit 2?
faqs.a: Apple's Swift-first framework for in-app purchases and subscriptions, using async/await. You fetch products, call purchase(), check that the result is verified, and read Transaction.currentEntitlements to know what the person owns.

faqs.q: How do I test in-app purchases without real money?
faqs.a: Use a StoreKit configuration file in Xcode to simulate the store, and later a Sandbox account on a real device. Test purchases, cancellations, refunds and renewals.

faqs.q: Does Vision send images to a server?
faqs.a: No. Vision analyses images on the device, which helps privacy and works offline. You still need to tell users what you do with any result you store.

quiz.q: When is a StoreKit 2 purchase treated as real?
options: As soon as the button is tapped

quiz.q: How can you test purchases without real money?
options: A StoreKit configuration file in Xcode

quiz.q: How many times must a checked continuation be resumed?

notes: StoreKit 2: `Product.products(for:)`, `product.purchase()`. Only a `.verified` result counts. Then `transaction.finish()`.
`Transaction.currentEntitlements` at launch, `Transaction.updates` for later changes. Offer Restore Purchases.
Test with a StoreKit configuration file, then a Sandbox account.
Vision runs on the device (text, faces, barcodes). Wrap completion handlers with `withCheckedThrowingContinuation`, resume exactly once.
AVFoundation: AVPlayer, AVAudioSession, AVCaptureSession (camera needs a usage description).
HealthKit: capability, usage description, ask per data type, strict rules on how data may be used.

lessons.title: Modular iOS Architecture: Swift Packages, Clean Architecture and Performance
lessons.metaTitle: Modular iOS Apps: SPM, Clean Architecture
lessons.description: Split a growing app into Swift packages, apply Clean Architecture layers, wire dependencies at one composition root, and profile launch, memory and scrolling.

content.text: A small app can live in one target. A big one cannot, for three reasons: builds get slow, any file can depend on any other so changes ripple everywhere, and several people cannot work in parallel without conflicts. **Modularisation** and a clear **architecture** are the answer, and *how would you structure a large app?* is a standard senior question. This lesson shows the practical version: Swift packages, layers, one place that wires everything, and the tools that find performance problems.
Swift Package Manager for your own code

Swift Package Manager (SPM) is built into Xcode. It adds third-party libraries, and it also lets you split *your own* code into **local packages**, each with its own tests. A package describes its targets in a `Package.swift` file.

items: Add it to the app with **File > Add Package Dependencies > Add Local**, then link the library to the app target.

Anything another module must see has to be marked **`public`**, including `init`s. The default access level, `internal`, hides things outside their own module. This is both the pain and the point of modules: they force you to decide what each one offers.
